prompt.context: Our client is a global CPG company with multiple lines of business (toothpaste, batteries, hair care, etc.). They are the global market leader in every market they play in, and have come to us specifically asking how they can grow their share in the razors and blades market.
prompt.question: What do you tell them? How can the client grow its share in the razors and blades market?

clarifying_info.q: How is the hair removal market segmented?
clarifying_info.a: The market is divided into wet-shaving and dry-hair removal (e.g., waxing, electric, etc.).

clarifying_info.q: How is wet shaving further divided?
clarifying_info.a: Wet shaving is divided into cartridge systems and disposables. The client has 70% of the men's shaving market and 35% of the women's cartridge-system market.

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of men use hair removal products regularly?
clarifying_info.a: 95% of men use hair removal products regularly.

clarifying_info.q: What is men's primary form of hair removal?
clarifying_info.a: 90% of men who use hair removal products shave as their primary form.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's share of the men's shaving market?
What percentage of women use hair removal products regularly?
clarifying_info.a: 90% of women use hair removal products regularly.

clarifying_info.q: What is women's primary form of hair removal?
clarifying_info.a: 70% of women who use hair removal products shave as their primary form.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's share of the women's shaving market?
clarifying_info.a: 50% overall (35% of cartridges and 65% of disposables).

clarifying_info.q: How do pricing tiers compare across product types?
clarifying_info.a: Disposable systems cost on average half the amount per shave as cartridge systems. Cartridge shaving costs on average half the amount per hair removal as dry-hair removal.

exhibits.title: Market Data Overview
exhibits.shows: Market share and segmentation data for the razors and blades market across genders and product types
exhibits.data: Client share men's shaving: 70%; Client share women's cartridge market: 35%; Market split between wet-shaving (cartridge, disposable) and dry-hair removal

framework: Segment the hair removal market: wet-shaving (cartridge, disposable) vs. dry-hair removal (waxing, electric)
Analyze client's current position by gender and product type to identify where share gaps exist
Quantify headroom for growth in each segment using market share and penetration data
Identify root causes limiting growth in underperforming segments
Develop strategies targeting the largest opportunity gaps (grow market, grow share within market, or improve pricing/mix)

questions.prompt: Based on the data provided, where does the client have the most room to grow?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate effective share of total hair-removal market by gender. For men: 95% use hair removal, 90% of those shave, client has 70% share of shavers → client reaches ~60% of all men who remove hair. For women: 90% use hair removal, 70% of those shave (so ~63% of all women), client has 50% of female shavers → client reaches ~31-35% of all women who remove hair. This reveals much more headroom in the women's segment. The candidate should also note that the client has high disposable share (65%) but low cartridge share (35%) among women, suggesting a mix opportunity.

math.setup: Calculate client's effective share of total hair-removal population by gender
steps: Men: 95% use hair removal × 90% shave = 85.5% of men who shave; client has 70% of shavers → 0.855 × 0.70 ≈ 60% of total male hair-removal users reached
Women: 90% use hair removal × 70% shave = 63% of women who shave; client has 50% of female shavers → 0.63 × 0.50 ≈ 31.5% of total female hair-removal users reached
Alternatively expressed: out of every 100 women who remove hair, client touches ~35; out of 100 men, client touches ~60
Women's cartridge share (35%) vs. disposable share (65%) shows heavy skew toward cheaper segment
math.answer: Client has ~60% effective reach among male hair-removal users vs. ~31-35% among female hair-removal users — the women's segment offers the most room to grow

questions.prompt: Why aren't more women using wet-shaving (specifically cartridge systems)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm demand-side barriers: fear of being cut, shaving perceived as a chore, shaving seen as masculine/unfeminine, shaving viewed as 'lower class' relative to waxing. These are attitudinal and cultural barriers rather than price or distribution barriers.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategies should the client pursue to grow its share in the women's razors and blades market?

categories.name: Grow total women's market (penetration)
ideas: Address fear of cuts with product design (e.g., safety features, moisturizing strips)
Reposition shaving as a modern, convenient grooming ritual
Target coastal/high-penetration regions first, then expand

categories.name: Grow share within existing women's shaving market
ideas: Encourage trade-up from disposables to cartridge systems (higher revenue per shave)
Loyalty programs or starter kit promotions for cartridge systems
Bundling with other personal care products in client's portfolio

categories.name: Increase revenue per user (price/mix)
ideas: Premiumize cartridge line to close price gap with dry-hair removal
Introduce marketing to shift perception of shaving up-market
Create premium women's sub-brand to command higher prices
Highlight cost-per-shave advantage vs. waxing/salon treatments

categories.name: Geographic expansion
ideas: Focus on countries/regions with high cultural affinity for shaving
Invest in markets where dry-hair removal dominates but wet-shave penetration is low

recommendation: Focus growth efforts on the women's segment, where the client reaches only ~31-35% of total hair-removal users versus ~60% for men

Prioritize two levers: (1) grow the total women's wet-shaving market by addressing attitudinal barriers (fear of cuts, masculine perception, class stigma) through targeted marketing, and (2) migrate existing women customers from disposables (65% share) to higher-value cartridge systems (35% share)
risks: Cultural/attitudinal barriers may be slow to shift and require sustained marketing investment
Premiumization could alienate cost-sensitive disposable users if not managed carefully
Competitors may react to any market expansion effort the client funds
next_steps: Quantify addressable revenue opportunity by segment to prioritize spend
Conduct consumer research on top attitudinal barriers by region
Design and pilot targeted marketing programs in high-potential markets
Track cartridge vs. disposable mix shift as a key performance metric
